items.question: In which year did Elisha Otis show a crowd that his elevator safety brake worked, by having the rope cut while he stood safely on the platform?
items.fact: At the 1854 Crystal Palace exhibition in New York, Elisha Otis rode a platform lift up and had the rope cut on purpose. His new safety brake caught the platform almost at once, and he was perfectly safe. That show helped people trust riding in elevators.

sources.title: Elevator history timeline - Otis Elevator
sources.quote: Standing high above the crowd on a platform lift, Otis orders the retaining rope to be cut. The platform drops a few inches and the crowd screams. But the safety brake immediately halts the descent.

sources.title: NIHF Inductee Elisha Otis Invented Elevator Brakes
sources.quote: In 1854, Otis dramatized his safety device on the floor of the Crystal Palace Exposition in New York. The inventor ascended in an elevator inside an open-sided shaft. Halfway up, he had the hoisting cable cut with an axe. The platform held fast.

verification.source_title: The Electric Elevator - IEEE REACH / IEEE History Center ETHW (PDF)
The Technological Breakthrough in Our Midst That Allowed Buildings To Grow Tall - Village Preservation

items.question: The first Otis passenger elevator was put into a New York shop called the Haughwout Building in 1857 - how many floors did that shop have?
items.fact: In 1857 Otis installed its first passenger elevator in the E.V. Haughwout Building, a five-floor department store at 488 Broadway in New York City.

sources.title: The Technological Breakthrough in Our Midst That Allowed Buildings To Grow Tall - Village Preservation
sources.quote: On March 23, 1857 the first Otis commercial passenger elevator was installed at 488 Broadway at Broome Street at the E.V. Haughwout Building. The elevator carried customers between the store's five floors.

items.question: Who built the world's first electric passenger elevator, in 1880?
items.fact: In 1880 Werner von Siemens built the world's first electric passenger elevator. It was the sensation of the Pfalzgau exhibition in Mannheim, Germany, where more than 8,000 visitors paid 20 pfennigs to ride it up the 20-metre observation tower of the customs office.

items.fact: In June 1889 five hydraulic lifts, pushed up by water pressure, went into service in the Eiffel Tower. Otis built the ones in the North and South pillars. Some of the tower's lifts are still hydraulic today, and the newer ones are electric.

items.question: A paternoster is a lift made of open cabins that go round in a loop without stopping - what do the Latin words 'pater noster' mean?
items.fact: 'Paternoster' is Latin for 'Our Father', the first words of the Lord's Prayer. The lift got the name because its cabins go round in a loop like a string of rosary prayer beads.

sources.title: The Paternoster Lift | EFM | The University of Sheffield
sources.quote: The name comes from system's resemblance to rosary prayer beads and is Latin for 'Our Father', which begins the Lord's Prayer.

sources.title: Paternoster lift - Wikipedia
sources.quote: The name paternoster ('Our Father', the first two words of the Lord's Prayer in Latin) was originally applied to the device because the elevator is in the form of a loop and is thus similar to rosary beads used as an aid in reciting prayers.

items.question: In ancient Rome, how were the lifts under the Colosseum's floor powered to raise scenery and animal cages up into the arena?
items.answer: Men pushing a winch round in a circle
items.fact: Under the Colosseum's floor were capstans - cross-shaped winches that teams of men pushed round as they walked in a circle - which lifted cages and scenery up through trapdoors into the arena. Researcher Heinz-Jürgen Beste of the German Archaeological Institute worked out that there were 60 of them.

sources.title: Secrets of the Colosseum - Smithsonian Magazine
sources.quote: At the peak of its operation, he concluded, the hypogeum contained 60 capstans, each two stories tall and turned by four men per level. Forty of these capstans lifted animal cages throughout the arena, while the remaining 20 were used to raise scenery sitting on hinged platforms measuring 12 by 15 feet.

verification.source_title: 1,500 Years Later, Killer Animal Elevator Returns to Colosseum | HISTORY
Secrets of the Colosseum - Smithsonian Magazine

items.question: Chicago's Home Insurance Building, often called the world's first skyscraper, was finished in 1885 with how many storeys?
items.fact: The Home Insurance Building in Chicago, completed in 1885, was 10 storeys (138 feet) tall. Much of its weight was carried by a metal frame skeleton - iron columns and beams, with some steel - rather than by thick stone walls alone. Safe elevators plus metal frames are what let buildings grow this tall.

sources.title: Home Insurance Building | Chicago Architecture Center
sources.quote: Completed in 1885 on LaSalle Street between Adams and Monroe, this 10-story structure employed innovative engineering techniques

items.question: An elevator's counterweight is as heavy as the empty car plus about what share of the biggest load the car is allowed to carry?
items.fact: Manufacturer TK Elevator explains that the counterweight is set to the empty cab's weight plus 40 to 50% of the rated load, so the motor only has to lift the difference. The counterweight travels up when the cab goes down and down when the cab goes up.

sources.title: Counterweights - TK Elevator Classroom On Demand
sources.quote: The weight of an elevator cab (structural load) plus part of the passenger load (40 to 50% of its rated load) determines the weight of the counterweights.

items.question: What pushes a hydraulic elevator car upward?
items.answer: A piston pushed by pumped fluid
distractors: A big spring in the pit
items.fact: In a hydraulic elevator a pump forces fluid into a cylinder, and the pressure pushes a piston that lifts the car. TK Elevator says hydraulic elevators are used for buildings with under 60 feet of travel, while taller buildings use traction elevators, where ropes or belts and a counterweight move the cab.

sources.title: Traction Elevators Vs. Hydraulic Elevators - TK Elevator
sources.quote: they use an electronic pump to push hydraulic fluid into a cylinder, using pressure. This pressure pushes a piston and causes the elevator to rise.

verification.source_title: Hydraulic vs. Traction Elevators for New Construction - Kaiser Elevator
Hydraulic Elevators: Here's How & Where They Work - Stanley Elevator

items.question: Under California's elevator rules, what is the fewest steel hoisting ropes a traction elevator is allowed to hang from?
items.fact: California's elevator safety rules (Title 8, section 3042) say a traction elevator must have at least three hoisting ropes, and together the ropes must be at least 7.6 times stronger than the loaded car needs, rising to nearly 12 times for the fastest elevators. The ropes are twisted steel cables that link the car to the counterweight over the drive sheave.

sources.title: Cal. Code Regs. Tit. 8, § 3042 — Hoisting Ropes and Their Connections (California DIR, Elevator Safety Orders)
sources.quote: The minimum number of hoisting ropes used shall be three for traction elevators, and two for drum-type elevators.

sources.title: Ropes (Hoists) - TK Elevator Classroom On Demand
sources.quote: These ropes are made from twisted fibers, often steel, to create a durable cord or cable which links the elevator cab sling to the counterweight and over the drive sheave.

verification.source_title: Cal. Code Regs. Title 8, Section 3042. Hoisting Ropes and Their Connections (California DIR)
Cal. Code Regs. Tit. 8, § 1604.25 — Hoisting and Counterweight Ropes (Construction Safety Orders, Cornell LII): the neighbouring rule, which governs construction HOISTS and stops at a factor of 10.70

items.question: Where are the cushioning buffers of a rope-driven elevator installed?
items.answer: In the pit at the bottom of the shaft
distractors: On top of the car's roof
items.fact: California's elevator rules say the buffers must sit in the pit under both the car and the counterweight. Spring buffers are fine for slower elevators, but when the rated speed is over 200 feet per minute the rules call for oil buffers (or something that works just as well).

sources.title: California Code of Regulations, Title 8, §3031. Car and Counterweight Buffers and Bumpers
sources.quote: Buffers or bumpers shall be installed under the cars and counterweights of all cable-driven power elevators.

verification.source_title: Cal. Code Regs. Tit. 8, § 3031 - Car and Counterweight Buffers and Bumpers | LII / Legal Information Institute

items.question: In what year did KONE launch MonoSpace, its elevator that needed no separate machine room?
items.fact: In 1996 KONE launched MonoSpace, which KONE calls the world's first machine-room-less elevator. Its flat, disc-shaped EcoDisc motor is thin enough to sit inside the hoistway, so the bulky machine no longer needed its own room at the top or bottom of the building.

items.question: What does an elevator's regenerative drive do with the electricity made when the car slows down?
items.answer: Feeds it back into the building's power supply
distractors: Turns it into heat in resistors
Sends it up the guide rails as light
items.fact: A traction elevator generates electricity when a lightly loaded car goes up, a heavy car goes down, or the car brakes. A regenerative drive sends that power back into the building's electrical grid instead of wasting it as heat in resistors; Otis says its ReGen drive cuts energy use by up to 75% compared with non-regenerative drives.

sources.title: ReGen Drives: The smart choice - Otis Elevator (brochure)
sources.quote: ReGen drives feed this energy back into the building's internal electrical grid where it can be used by other loads or users connected to the same network.

sources.title: Elevator history timeline - Otis Elevator
sources.quote: Otis adds its ReGen drive...as standard in all Gen2 elevators...enables energy savings.

items.question: What do many elevator doors use to spot someone standing in the doorway and open again without touching them?
distractors: A weighing scale in the floor
items.fact: Modern elevator doors shine many infrared light beams across the opening; if a person or bag breaks a beam, the doors stop and reopen. US accessibility rules say this reopening device must work without needing physical contact.

sources.title: 2010 ADA Standards, Section 407.3 Elevator Doors (corada)
sources.quote: The device shall not require physical contact to be activated, although contact is permitted to occur before the door reverses.

items.question: In most US elevators, why can't pressing the 'door close' button make the doors shut right away?
items.answer: A law says the doors must stay open for a few seconds so everyone has time to get in
distractors: The button only switches on the ceiling light
The doors are too heavy to move any faster
The button only works on the top floor
items.fact: Because of the 1990 Americans with Disabilities Act, US elevator doors must stay fully open for at least 3 seconds after a button inside the car is pressed, so people using wheelchairs or crutches have time to board. The 'door close' button cannot cut that wait short; once the required wait is over, it can work.

sources.quote: "The riding public would not be able to make those doors close any faster," Penafiel told The Times.

sources.quote: Penafiel says the buttons' function changed in 1990 when the Americans with Disability Act instituted rules giving those with mobility issues more time to get onto the elevator.

sources.title: 2010 ADA Standards, Section 407.3.5 Door Delay (corada)
sources.quote: Elevator doors shall remain fully open in response to a car call for 3 seconds minimum.

items.question: What do people in Britain call the machine that Americans call an elevator?
items.fact: Britons, Australians, Irish, New Zealanders and South Africans say 'lift', while Americans and Canadians say 'elevator'. 'Lift' comes from the Old Norse word 'lypta' (to raise) and 'elevator' from the Latin 'elevare' (to raise up).

items.question: Hitachi's lift in the Guangzhou CTF Finance Centre, the world's fastest in 2019, is rated at 1,260 metres per minute. How many metres per second is that?
items.fact: 1,260 divided by 60 is 21, so the lift climbs 21 metres every second. Guinness World Records certified it as the world's fastest elevator on 10 September 2019; it goes from the ground floor to the 95th floor, a 440 m trip, in about 42 seconds.

items.question: In 2017 thyssenkrupp (now TK Elevator) showed off MULTI, the first rope-free elevator for tall buildings. Besides up and down, which way can its cabins also move?

It took its first ride on 22 June 2017 in TK Elevator's 246 m test tower in Rottweil, Germany. As of 2024 it was still being tested there and had not yet been fitted in a real building.

items.question: Each Gateway Arch tram in St. Louis is a train of 8 little capsules with 5 seats each. How many people can ride in one tram?
items.fact: 8 times 5 is 40. Dick Bowser designed the trams by combining an elevator with a Ferris wheel so the capsules stay upright as they follow the Arch's curve. The north tram opened in July 1967 and the south tram in May 1968. The ride to the top of the 630-foot (192 m) Arch takes 4 minutes up and 3 minutes down.

items.question: A giant steel ball hangs near the top of Taipei 101 to cut down how much the tower sways in the wind. How much does the ball weigh?

It was the world's largest tuned mass damper when the tower opened on 31 December 2004, and Guinness still lists it that way, but Shanghai Tower in China now has a heavier one weighing about 1,000 tonnes.

items.fact: 103,000 divided by 40,000 is a little over 2.5, which matches the tower's own figure of two and a half times around the world every year. Two of the tower's lifts were first installed in 1899 and, after several modernisations, still carry visitors today.

items.question: A 'space elevator' would be a cable running from the ground up to a station in geostationary orbit, the orbit where a satellite stays above the same spot on Earth. About how high up is that orbit?
items.fact: Geostationary orbit is about 35,786 km up. A NASA report in 2000 said an Earth-to-orbit space elevator 'is not feasible today' because no material we can make yet is strong and light enough for such a long cable; carbon nanotubes, measured in the lab at about 100 times the strength of steel, are the hoped-for material.

items.question: Muzak, the company whose name became a nickname for 'elevator music', got that name by mixing 'music' with the name of which company?
items.fact: The name Muzak dates from 1934. The company grew out of a 'wired radio' music service based on inventions by US Army general George Owen Squier, and the new name blends 'music' with the ending of the camera brand 'Kodak'. The name became so well known that people now call any gentle background music 'Muzak' or 'elevator music'.

items.question: In which century did the Indian mathematician Brahmagupta write down rules for doing sums with zero?
items.fact: In the 7th century the Indian mathematician Brahmagupta wrote down rules for arithmetic with zero, such as 'the sum of zero and zero is zero'. Much earlier, by around 300-400 BC, Babylonian scribes were putting two little wedge marks in the place where we would write a 0 - a placeholder, not yet a number in its own right.

items.question: Which of these numbers is NOT a prime number?
items.fact: A prime number is a whole number bigger than 1 that can only be divided by 1 and itself, so 1 is not counted as prime. Leaving 1 out means every number can be built from primes in exactly one way.

sources.title: Wolfram MathWorld: Prime Number
sources.quote: A prime number (or prime integer, often simply called a 'prime' for short) is a positive integer p>1 that has no positive integer divisors other than 1 and p itself.

sources.title: Wolfram MathWorld: Prime Number (why 1 is excluded)
sources.quote: A good reason not to call 1 a prime number is that if 1 were prime, then the statement of the fundamental theorem of arithmetic would have to be modified since 'in exactly one' way would be false because any n=n·1.

verification.source_title: PrimePages (t5k.org): Why is the number one not prime?

items.question: How many zeros come after the 1 in a googol?
items.fact: A googol is a 1 followed by 100 zeros (10 to the power 100). The name was invented by mathematician Edward Kasner's nine-year-old nephew, Milton Sirotta, when he was asked to think up a name for a very big number.

items.question: 6 is a perfect number because 1 + 2 + 3 = 6. What is the next perfect number after 6?
items.fact: A perfect number equals the sum of its divisors, not counting itself. 28 = 1 + 2 + 4 + 7 + 14. The first four perfect numbers are 6, 28, 496 and 8,128.

items.question: A palindromic number reads the same forwards and backwards. Which of these is a palindromic number?
items.fact: A palindromic number is the same when written forwards or backwards, like 121 or 12321. Every one-digit number counts, and the first two-digit ones are 11, 22, 33 and so on up to 99.

items.question: Which number has no symbol of its own in Roman numerals?
items.fact: Roman numerals use the letters I, V, X, L, C, D and M (for 1, 5, 10, 50, 100, 500 and 1000) but have no symbol for zero and no place value, which made sums hard. More than 2,000 years ago the Babylonians were the first to use a mark for an 'empty place' in a number - the very beginning of zero.

items.question: In the old wheat-and-chessboard puzzle, 1 grain goes on square 1, 2 on square 2, 4 on square 3, doubling every square. How many digits long is the number of grains on all 64 squares?
items.fact: Doubling 63 times and adding it all up gives 2^64 minus 1 = 18,446,744,073,709,551,615 grains — a number 20 digits long. Doubling makes numbers grow astonishingly fast.

items.question: If you start at 1 and double it 10 times, what number do you reach?
items.fact: Doubling 1 ten times gives 2^10 = 1,024. Because 1,024 is so close to 1,000, computer people often use 'kilo' to mean 1,024 instead of 1,000. To keep the two apart, in 1998 an international standards group (the IEC) gave 1,024 its own name: 1,024 bits is a 'kibibit'.

items.question: What is the classic reason manhole covers are made round rather than square?
items.answer: A round cover cannot fall through its own hole
distractors: Round covers keep rain out better
Round covers are easier to see at night
items.fact: A circle is the same width whichever way you turn it, so a round cover can never slip through its own round hole. A square cover tipped on its diagonal could drop through, because a square's diagonal is about 1.414 times as long as its side. Round covers have other perks too: they can be rolled along, and they never need turning to fit.

sources.title: Round Manhole Cover - P2SL Mistake-Proofing, UC Berkeley
sources.quote: A round cover cannot fall through a circular opening of at least the same diameter, no matter how it is positioned.

sources.title: The Surprisingly Technical Reason That Manhole Covers Are Round - Enviro Design Products
sources.quote: if you have a square cover, the diagonal distance across the length of the square is 1.414 times the length of the sides ... if you were to drop a square cover onto its opening at a diagonal angle, it could easily fall through.

verification.source_title: Why Are Most Manhole Covers Circular And Not Triangular, Square Or Rectangular? - ScienceABC
Manhole cover - Wikipedia

items.question: Which ancient people counted in sixties, and are usually credited with giving us the 360-degree circle?
items.fact: The Babylonians used a positional base-60 number system, and our 360-degree circle harks back to them. Nobody knows for certain why 360 was chosen: it is 6 times 60, and it is also close to the number of days in a year, so the Sun seems to move about one degree along its path each day.

sources.title: Degree - Wolfram MathWorld

items.question: Which shape of room divides a flat surface into equal-sized rooms using the least total wall?
items.fact: Maths has a rule called the honeycomb conjecture: if you divide a flat surface into rooms that are all the same size, no pattern uses less wall than a grid of regular hexagons. Thomas Hales proved it in 1999. Whether bees build hexagons for this reason is a separate question about bees, not maths.

sources.quote: The classical honeycomb conjecture asserts that any partition of the plane into regions of equal area has perimeter at least that of the regular hexagonal honeycomb tiling.

items.fact: Binary is the base-2 way of counting using only the digits 0 and 1. Computers use it because every number can be stored as a string of electrical ons and offs. The German thinker Gottfried Leibniz had worked out binary arithmetic by 1679.

items.question: How many sides does a Möbius strip have?
items.fact: A Möbius strip is made by giving a paper band a half twist before joining its ends. The result has only one side and one edge. Two mathematicians, August Möbius and Johann Listing, each found it on their own in 1858. Listing wrote about it first, but the strip is named after Möbius.

sources.quote: The Möbius strip, also called the twisted cylinder (Henle 1994, p. 110), is a one-sided nonorientable surface obtained by cutting a closed band into a single strip, giving one of the two ends thus produced a half twist, and then reattaching the two ends ... The strip bearing his name was invented by Möbius in 1858, although it was independently discovered by Listing, who published it, while Möbius did not

items.question: A classic symmetrical snowflake has how many arms or sides?
items.fact: A classic snow crystal has six-fold symmetry, with six sides or six arms. That symmetry comes from the way water molecules are arranged in the ice crystal lattice, which is hexagonal.

items.question: An empty elevator car weighs 1000 kg and its counterweight weighs 1500 kg. Then 300 kg of people get in. Now how much heavier is the counterweight than the car with the people inside?
items.fact: An elevator counterweight is usually set to the weight of the empty car plus 40 to 50% of the load the elevator is rated to carry. It moves the opposite way to the car, so the motor only has to lift the difference in weight. Here the car with people weighs 1000 + 300 = 1300 kg, and 1500 - 1300 = 200 kg.

sources.title: Counterweights - TK Elevator Classroom On Demand
sources.quote: The weight of an elevator cab (structural load) plus part of the passenger load (40 to 50% of its rated load) determines the weight of the counterweights. ... The weights travel up and down in the opposite direction from the elevator cab.

items.question: The Burj Khalifa's fastest elevators climb 10 metres every second; if each floor were 4 metres tall, how many floors would they pass each second?
items.fact: Otis's double-deck elevators in the Burj Khalifa run at up to 10 metres per second (as of 2024) and reach the observation deck on floors 124 and 125 in about 60 seconds. If each floor were 4 metres tall, 10 divided by 4 would give 2.5 floors every second.

sources.quote: Two double-deck elevators travel at speeds of up to 10 meters per second, taking passengers from the ground floor to the observation deck on the 124th and 125th floors in just 60 seconds.

items.question: To do 9 times 4 on your hands you hold up ten fingers and fold down the 4th finger from the left; fingers to its left are tens and fingers to its right are ones, so what answer do you get?
items.fact: With the 4th finger folded down, three fingers stand to its left (the tens) and six to its right (the ones), giving 36, which is 9 times 4. The trick works for 9 times 1 up to 9 times 10, one for each finger.

sources.title: Multiplication Tricks - UVU Math Lab, Utah Valley University
sources.quote: Hand Method: 1. Hold up ten fingers. 2. Count over from the left the number of fingers equal to the multiplier. 3. Hold that finger down. 4. The number of fingers to the left of the multiplier is the tens place of the solution. 5. The number of fingers to the right is in the ones place of the solution.

items.question: In what year did Robert Recorde first print the equals sign, =, in a maths book?
items.fact: Robert Recorde introduced the = sign in his 1557 book The Whetstone of Witte. He chose a pair of parallel lines 'bicause noe .2. thynges, can be moare equalle' (because no two things can be more equal).

items.question: If you fold a sheet of A4 paper in half so its two short edges meet, what paper size is the folded sheet?
items.fact: Every sheet in the A series is the same shape: its long side is about 1.4 times its short side (the square root of 2). Because of that, halving a sheet's longer side gives two smaller sheets of exactly the same shape. A4 is 210 by 297 mm, and half of it is A5, 148 by 210 mm.

sources.title: International standard paper sizes - Markus Kuhn, University of Cambridge Computer Laboratory
sources.quote: In the ISO paper size system, the height-to-width ratio of all pages is the square root of two (1.4142 : 1). ... cut one parallel to its shorter side into two equal pieces, then the resulting page will have again the same width/height ratio. ... A4 210 × 297
